Road Accident Benefit Scheme - who will be benefiting?

By: Este de Klerk | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Quite soon, the Road Accident Fund will be replaced when the new Bill on the Road Accident Benefit Scheme is signed into power. What will change and what does it mean for the victims of car accidents?

Summary:
Quite soon, the Road Accident Fund will be replaced when the new Bill on the Road Accident Benefit Scheme is signed into power. What will change and what does it mean for the victims of car accidents?

For years, the current Road Accident Fund (RAF) has been riddled with controversy - from lawyers like Bobroff taking much more than they are eligible to from the innocent victims of car accidents whose lives have been changed forever, to billions of rands of outstanding claims due to alleged mismanagement and incompetence at the organisation.

Further information:
The proposed Bill for the Road Accident Benefit Scheme that will replace the RAF, will be signed into power at Parliament soon.
It is an initiative from and will be implemented by the Department of Transport and the RAF is quick to defend that they are only following government's procedures and new initiative.

The RAF is currently in a R144-billion deficit and has a backlog of 176-thousand outstanding cases. The new system will be managed by an Administrator and the backlog needs to be cleared, despite more cases that will be instituted due to the new Road Accident Benefit Scheme that also allow the person who was responsible for the accident to claim from the fund. This will ultimately increase the claim load and leave less money to be paid out to victims of car accidents who really need it to be cared for.

The Road Accident Fund (RAF) was established in 1996 to protect the rights of innocent persons injured in accidents as a result of another’s negligent driving. The fund was designed to compensate victims for damages incurred, pain and suffering, medical expenses and loss of income, and also to protect those dependents who suffered loss of support due to a provider’s injury or death.

The RAF is funded by fuel levies. For every rand paid for petrol, a percentage is set aside for the fund. The fund therefore should be well supported and maintained with continual growth as road use increases year by year. Those able to prove injuries and expenses incurred as a result of an accident that was not their fault, could apply and expect fair assessment and compensation for costs and/or loss of income to be paid out in a lump sum.

The problems with RAF:
However, over the years a number of problems developed with regard to the application process through the RAF. Chief of these included unacceptable delays in processing claims, often not at all unless the case was pursued by attorney. Delays of up to 55 months before a victim might receive compensation – and then only when professional assistance was sought by a claimant – were eroding the purpose and fairness of the ‘raison d’etre’ for the fund’s existence.

Because of this incompetence, many claims would only be paid out if litigation was involved, resulting not only in extensive time delays but also unnecessary costs. This maladministration bled money from the fund, and compensation that should have been efficiently assessed and paid out in a reasonable time-span, was instead spent on time-consuming processes through the courts.

So, undeniably, change was required. And this change has finally surfaced in the form of the Road Accident Benefit Scheme proposed to replace RAF. The draft RABS bill was published in May 2014. While seeking to institute a fairer spread of compensation to benefit the unemployed, or those earning below the Annual National Average Income (AANI), RABS brings with it a number of negative implications, such as:

• All claims need to be submitted electronically in order to be considered.
• The ‘No Fault’ system is supported – which means that the person who caused the accident will also be able to claim for injuries sustained.
• If you don’t hear from RABS for 180 days after submitting your claim, your claim has been denied.
• There is no lump sum payment – benefits are reduced to small monthly payments.
• Loss of long-term ‘career path’ earnings are no longer considered – ie: loss of income (LOI) that would have been in your life had there been no accident, are not relevant.
• LOI benefits will be based on only 75% of the claimant’s earnings prior to the accident.
• Benefits are not inflation-linked nor guaranteed as benefits can be reviewed, revised or suspended at any time.
• Claimants access to attorneys is limited, therefore the constitutional right to access the courts is denied.
• The nature and extent of a victim’s medical treatment will be decided by the RABS Administrator.
• There will be no general damage claims for pain and suffering.
• There will be no financial assistance for any legal or administrative costs the victim may incur while trying process their claim.
• Costs of obtaining medical and police reports will lie with the claimant – RABS will not refund these costs.
• The claims of children, persons over 60 years of age, and persons earning over R220,000 pa, will be limited to emergency medical care only.
• Funeral expenses will be limited to R10,000.
• Benefits terminate on the death of the claimant, leaving any dependents without support.
• Benefits terminate after 15 years or when the claimant reaches 60, whichever comes first.
• Stringent rules will apply to qualify for long-term medical care – and will only be allowed from healthcare contractors specified by the RABS administration.

Press Release:


RABS vs RAF
The Minister of Transport has published the Road Accident Benefit Scheme (RABS) bill. If implemented, the scheme would replace the current Road Accident Fund in the hope that it brings an end to needless litigation and delays. But according to experts, the new proposal is riddled with controversy. The no-fault based RABS system means even reckless drivers are entitled to claim, while injured victims can no longer recover full losses suffered. Carte Blanche asks: how will it work and who exactly will benefit?


Script:


RABS SCRIPT

PRODUCER: ESTÉ DE KLERK

[start with accident]

Most of us have probably had a minor car accident somewhere in our lives.
Many of us know someone who’s been in a more serious one.

In such cases, the damage caused to vehicles is insignificant in comparison to death or serious injuries that could change lives forever.


THABO RAMAILA: When you are being told you are a quadriplegic, that is not a problem. Living as a quadriplegic, that is when you see a crisis.

THABANG CINDI: He was like a normal brother, he was smart. After the accident he was not the brother that I knew.

IRENE FISCHER: I don’t think about it often, but I do think like: where would I have been now.

On South African roads , 41 people die every day.
Many more are severely injured, often resulting in serious financial and personal losses.
But, the right to sue the person who caused your accident, was abolished in 2008.

This is where the Road Accident Fund comes in.
Funded through a percentage of the fuel levy every time you fill up – the RAF compensates victims for personal injury losses suffered, medical expenses, loss of income and general damages - paid as a lump sum.
Claims against the RAF are processed and lodged in a court by an attorney on a victim’s behalf.

Now government wants to change this system, and the Draft Bill may soon be signed into law.

DEVI LINK: It’s called the Road Accident Benefit Scheme which will replace the Road Accident Fund. But who exactly will benefit?

In comparison to the RAF, RABS would be based on a no-fault-system – allowing the person who caused the accident an equal right to claim.

Claimants can no longer be represented by an attorney, which means
you will have to prepare, lodge and champion your own claim.
There will be no lump sum payment anymore, but only defined and prescribed funeral, medical, family and income support benefits.
The income support benefit will end after 15 years or the age 60, whichever comes first.

THABO RAMAILA: I was in denial. I said: you are not God, you are not going to tell me if I am going to walk or not
a week past, a month, a second month and then I was transferred to a rehabilitation centre.

As Thabo Rama ila rolls down the streets of Soshanguve, he often comtemplates what his life would have been like - had he not become a quadriplegic in an accident in 2007 when he was a student.

While Thabo was in rehab, his mom, Grace went directly to the RAF to claim on her son’s behalf and was only offered R25 000.
She approached an attorney and in 2013, the RAF settled, paying Thabo R4 million.

THABO RAMAILA: I am not walking, but I feel much, much better, I can live on, I can do what everyone is doing,

Irene Fischer was a radio presenter at OFM in Bloemfontein when her car was hit by a truck in 2009. Apart from other physical injuries, she sustained a traumatic brain injury, damaging every part of her brain except her intellect. She had to re-learn how to walk, eat, talk and write.

IRENE: I thought I was going to heal, to get better, and then I think, it was only in 2011 that I realized, it’s been like more than a year after the accident, things is remaining difficult to do – many things – and only then did I realize: okay, this is my life.

After four years of litigation, the RAF settled her case at R8,2 million, of which just over 6 million was paid to her.

Thabiso Cindi was seven in 1991 when he was run over by a car. He sustained severe brain injuries and now has the mental capacity of a ten-year old. The RAF paid him a lump sum of only R100 000.
Years later, Thabiso’s brother, Thabang, questioned this amount, which he considered to be a very low settlement.

THABANG: It really bothered me why people didn’t get his money. Get a reasonable amount of money, because brain injury is irreversable.

While researching Thabiso’s case, in 2013, he met Anthony Millar, the President of the Law Society of the Northern Provinces.

LINK: Anthony re-opened the case, which was settled a weeks ago at 28 times the original settlement amount.

Under the proposed RABS regulations, it will not be possible for people like Irene , Thabo and Thabiso to claim lump sum payments like they did from the current RAF.
Someone injured as a child, like Thabiso, will under the new RABS scheme, not be entitled to lodge a claim for income support benefits until they reach the age of 18, but the child will be entitled to medical expenses.

ANTHONY MILLAR: The current system has difficulties, but we know what they are, we can see them and we can address them. We use the mechanism of the court and the law to compel the RAF to do what it needs to do in the interest of our clients.

But the RAF’s head of legal, compliance and regulation, Charlene Louw, says the system is in need of an overhall.

CHARLENE LOUW: The RAF has been bankrupt for many many years. We unfortunately are part of a system that is essentially driven by a process that is costing us from an administrative perspective and it is just far too burdensome to continue in its current form.

The organisation has been dogged by maladministration for many years.
Despite employing 530 new workers over the past two years, the Fund still has 188-thousand old and new cases in the system.
During the past three financials years, the RAF received R67,5 billion - but still has a real deficit of 10,5 billion and an acturial AK-CHOO-AIR-EE-UL deficit of 144 billion.

Even judges have expressed their concern.

JUDGE EBERHARD BERTELSMANN: The compensation of road accident victims requires a radical change that should be free of the shackles of an institution that does neither comply with its duty to uphold the fundamental rights enshrined in the Constitution nor with the duties imposed upon it by its statute.

CHARLENE: The system is riddled with fraud, uncertain outcomes because of the litigation processes associated around it and claimants that are not always receiving the benefit that is due to them and the compensation that has been paid out by the RAF.

DEVI LINK: One of the biggest criticism against the Road Accident Fund is that they are responsible for dragging out the cases, leading to wasteful expenditure, but often settling on the steps of the court.

ANTHONY: Offers are made on the day of the trial, they are not made six weeks before, or six months before, as one would expect.

CHARLENE: An offer then gets made to the attorney of the claimant, who often then rejects it, hoping the court process would reap a bigger amount of money for their client.


The RABS draft Bill states loss of income benefits would be determined between a minimum and maximum cap, based on the national average income.

Unemployed people, like Thabo who was studying when his accident happened, will only be rewarded R44 000 per annum, paid in monthly installments of R3 700 per month.

THABO: That is an insult to someone’s life. That’s when they prove it to you, your life is done, you are done.

Under the the new RABS legislation, someome like Irene who was employed and earned more than the maximum capped amount, will qualify for R220 per year, the maximum income benefit which translates into R18 300 per month.

CHARLENE LOUW: Even when you are earning R500 000, there must be an assumption that you are able to self-insure. We want to make sure that the spread of the benefit goes to those that in any event would not have been able to self-insure.

ANTHONY MILLAR: if you have a situation like RABS, where you have a flat rate and a minimal amount, what you are basically doing, is you are condemning people to a particular socio-economic situation.

DEVI: All these benefits will last 15 years or until you turn 60 years, whichever comes first? And what must you do after that?

CHARLENE LOUW: There are other agencies within the state that would deal with those particular individuals within the social development basket of grants.

DEVI: You mean an old-age grant, a child grant and using the state hospital service?

CHARLENE LOUW: Yes

And if you’re in an accident and you’re already 60, you can only claim for medical expenses and not for any loss of income.

CHARLENE LOUW: The system cannot carry an individual for life.

Thabo and Irene both say they doubt the proposed monthly payment system will work. They’ve both been let-down by the RAF’s ill-administration in the past.
Part of their court settlements were undertakings by the RAF to provide them each with two caregivers.
Thabo pays a care agency himself, but hasn’t been refunded once in the past ten months.
Irene’s care givers have only been paid three times since 2013.

DEVI LINK: The proposed no-fault system means that reckless driving will be rewarded. Bad drivers are actually encouraged to also now claim.

Countries like Canada, Australia and the USA also operate on a no-fault system.
But the USA, with a population of over 323 million, only has 13,6 accidents per 100 000 vehicles.
South Africa with a population 7 times smaller, has 165 accidents per 100 000.

DEVI: This proposed no-fault system then means that there is no liability on the person who drives recklessly and causes an accident?

CHARLENE LOUW: The sense of responsibility has to be towards those individuals that are dependant on somebody for survival and therefore when that person no longer is there, what happens to that family? Someone has to look after them.

DEVI: But it will also double the number of applications that you are going to get?

CHARLENE LOUW: It does, but that is exactly what we would like to see

ANTHONY: RABS is a kite, but it is not going to fly.



PROMO’S

PROMO 1: 15”
You can’t use an attorney to handle your claim.
You won’t get a lump sum payment.
Your income benefit will be capped and cease after 15 years.

It’s called the Road Accident Benefit Scheme and will replace the Road Accident Fund if signed into law.


PROMO 2: 15”
South Africa has the highest accident rate in the world.
But if the Draft Bill of the Road Accident Benefit Scheme is signed into law to replace our current Road Accident Fund, reckless drivers will be able to claim for the same benefits as the victim of the accident.


PROMO 3: 10”

DEVI: It’s called the Road Accident Benefit Scheme which will replace the Road Accident Fund. But who exactly will benefit?

ANTHONY: It will not benefit the poor, it will benefit nobody.

04 April 2016 Press Release: RABS vs RAF The Minister of Transport has published the Road Accident Benefit Scheme (RABS) bill. If implemented, the scheme would replace the current Road Accident Fund in the hope that it brings an end to needless litigation and delays. But according to experts, the new proposal is riddled with controversy. The no-fault based RABS system means even reckless drivers are entitled to claim, while injured victims can no longer recover full losses suffered. Carte Blanche asks: how will it work and who exactly will benefit? Script: RABS SCRIPT PRODUCER: ESTÉ DE KLERK [start with accident] Most of us have probably had a minor car accident somewhere in our lives. Many of us know someone who’s been in a more serious one. In such cases, the damage caused to vehicles is insignificant in comparison to death or serious injuries that could change lives forever. THABO RAMAILA: When you are being told you are a quadriplegic, that is not a problem. Living as a quadriplegic, that is when you see a crisis. THABANG CINDI: He was like a normal brother, he was smart. After the accident he was not the brother that I knew. IRENE FISCHER: I don’t think about it often, but I do think like: where would I have been now. On South African roads , 41 people die every day. Many more are severely injured, often resulting in serious financial and personal losses. But, the right to sue the person who caused your accident, was abolished in 2008. This is where the Road Accident Fund comes in. Funded through a percentage of the fuel levy every time you fill up – the RAF compensates victims for personal injury losses suffered, medical expenses, loss of income and general damages - paid as a lump sum. Claims against the RAF are processed and lodged in a court by an attorney on a victim’s behalf. Now government wants to change this system, and the Draft Bill may soon be signed into law. DEVI LINK: It’s called the Road Accident Benefit Scheme which will replace the Road Accident Fund. But who exactly will benefit? In comparison to the RAF, RABS would be based on a no-fault-system – allowing the person who caused the accident an equal right to claim. Claimants can no longer be represented by an attorney, which means you will have to prepare, lodge and champion your own claim. There will be no lump sum payment anymore, but only defined and prescribed funeral, medical, family and income support benefits. The income support benefit will end after 15 years or the age 60, whichever comes first. THABO RAMAILA: I was in denial. I said: you are not God, you are not going to tell me if I am going to walk or not a week past, a month, a second month and then I was transferred to a rehabilitation centre. As Thabo Rama ila rolls down the streets of Soshanguve, he often comtemplates what his life would have been like - had he not become a quadriplegic in an accident in 2007 when he was a student. While Thabo was in rehab, his mom, Grace went directly to the RAF to claim on her son’s behalf and was only offered R25 000. She approached an attorney and in 2013, the RAF settled, paying Thabo R4 million. THABO RAMAILA: I am not walking, but I feel much, much better, I can live on, I can do what everyone is doing, Irene Fischer was a radio presenter at OFM in Bloemfontein when her car was hit by a truck in 2009. Apart from other physical injuries, she sustained a traumatic brain injury, damaging every part of her brain except her intellect. She had to re-learn how to walk, eat, talk and write. IRENE: I thought I was going to heal, to get better, and then I think, it was only in 2011 that I realized, it’s been like more than a year after the accident, things is remaining difficult to do – many things – and only then did I realize: okay, this is my life. After four years of litigation, the RAF settled her case at R8,2 million, of which just over 6 million was paid to her. Thabiso Cindi was seven in 1991 when he was run over by a car. He sustained severe brain injuries and now has the mental capacity of a ten-year old. The RAF paid him a lump sum of only R100 000. Years later, Thabiso’s brother, Thabang, questioned this amount, which he considered to be a very low settlement. THABANG: It really bothered me why people didn’t get his money. Get a reasonable amount of money, because brain injury is irreversable. While researching Thabiso’s case, in 2013, he met Anthony Millar, the President of the Law Society of the Northern Provinces. LINK: Anthony re-opened the case, which was settled a weeks ago at 28 times the original settlement amount. Under the proposed RABS regulations, it will not be possible for people like Irene , Thabo and Thabiso to claim lump sum payments like they did from the current RAF. Someone injured as a child, like Thabiso, will under the new RABS scheme, not be entitled to lodge a claim for income support benefits until they reach the age of 18, but the child will be entitled to medical expenses. ANTHONY MILLAR: The current system has difficulties, but we know what they are, we can see them and we can address them. We use the mechanism of the court and the law to compel the RAF to do what it needs to do in the interest of our clients. But the RAF’s head of legal, compliance and regulation, Charlene Louw, says the system is in need of an overhall. CHARLENE LOUW: The RAF has been bankrupt for many many years. We unfortunately are part of a system that is essentially driven by a process that is costing us from an administrative perspective and it is just far too burdensome to continue in its current form. The organisation has been dogged by maladministration for many years. Despite employing 530 new workers over the past two years, the Fund still has 188-thousand old and new cases in the system. During the past three financials years, the RAF received R67,5 billion - but still has a real deficit of 10,5 billion and an acturial AK-CHOO-AIR-EE-UL deficit of 144 billion. Even judges have expressed their concern. JUDGE EBERHARD BERTELSMANN: The compensation of road accident victims requires a radical change that should be free of the shackles of an institution that does neither comply with its duty to uphold the fundamental rights enshrined in the Constitution nor with the duties imposed upon it by its statute. CHARLENE: The system is riddled with fraud, uncertain outcomes because of the litigation processes associated around it and claimants that are not always receiving the benefit that is due to them and the compensation that has been paid out by the RAF. DEVI LINK: One of the biggest criticism against the Road Accident Fund is that they are responsible for dragging out the cases, leading to wasteful expenditure, but often settling on the steps of the court. ANTHONY: Offers are made on the day of the trial, they are not made six weeks before, or six months before, as one would expect. CHARLENE: An offer then gets made to the attorney of the claimant, who often then rejects it, hoping the court process would reap a bigger amount of money for their client. The RABS draft Bill states loss of income benefits would be determined between a minimum and maximum cap, based on the national average income. Unemployed people, like Thabo who was studying when his accident happened, will only be rewarded R44 000 per annum, paid in monthly installments of R3 700 per month. THABO: That is an insult to someone’s life. That’s when they prove it to you, your life is done, you are done. Under the the new RABS legislation, someome like Irene who was employed and earned more than the maximum capped amount, will qualify for R220 per year, the maximum income benefit which translates into R18 300 per month. CHARLENE LOUW: Even when you are earning R500 000, there must be an assumption that you are able to self-insure. We want to make sure that the spread of the benefit goes to those that in any event would not have been able to self-insure. ANTHONY MILLAR: if you have a situation like RABS, where you have a flat rate and a minimal amount, what you are basically doing, is you are condemning people to a particular socio-economic situation. DEVI: All these benefits will last 15 years or until you turn 60 years, whichever comes first? And what must you do after that? CHARLENE LOUW: There are other agencies within the state that would deal with those particular individuals within the social development basket of grants. DEVI: You mean an old-age grant, a child grant and using the state hospital service? CHARLENE LOUW: Yes And if you’re in an accident and you’re already 60, you can only claim for medical expenses and not for any loss of income. CHARLENE LOUW: The system cannot carry an individual for life. Thabo and Irene both say they doubt the proposed monthly payment system will work. They’ve both been let-down by the RAF’s ill-administration in the past. Part of their court settlements were undertakings by the RAF to provide them each with two caregivers. Thabo pays a care agency himself, but hasn’t been refunded once in the past ten months. Irene’s care givers have only been paid three times since 2013. DEVI LINK: The proposed no-fault system means that reckless driving will be rewarded. Bad drivers are actually encouraged to also now claim. Countries like Canada, Australia and the USA also operate on a no-fault system. But the USA, with a population of over 323 million, only has 13,6 accidents per 100 000 vehicles. South Africa with a population 7 times smaller, has 165 accidents per 100 000. DEVI: This proposed no-fault system then means that there is no liability on the person who drives recklessly and causes an accident? CHARLENE LOUW: The sense of responsibility has to be towards those individuals that are dependant on somebody for survival and therefore when that person no longer is there, what happens to that family? Someone has to look after them. DEVI: But it will also double the number of applications that you are going to get? CHARLENE LOUW: It does, but that is exactly what we would like to see ANTHONY: RABS is a kite, but it is not going to fly. PROMO’S PROMO 1: 15” You can’t use an attorney to handle your claim. You won’t get a lump sum payment. Your income benefit will be capped and cease after 15 years. It’s called the Road Accident Benefit Scheme and will replace the Road Accident Fund if signed into law. PROMO 2: 15” South Africa has the highest accident rate in the world. But if the Draft Bill of the Road Accident Benefit Scheme is signed into law to replace our current Road Accident Fund, reckless drivers will be able to claim for the same benefits as the victim of the accident. PROMO 3: 10” DEVI: It’s called the Road Accident Benefit Scheme which will replace the Road Accident Fund. But who exactly will benefit? ANTHONY: It will not benefit the poor, it will benefit nobody.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Quite soon, the Road Accident Fund will be replaced when the new Bill on the Road Accident Benefit Scheme is signed into power. What will change and what does it mean for the victims of car accidents?
metadata.Summary: Quite soon, the Road Accident Fund will be replaced when the new Bill on the Road Accident Benefit Scheme is signed into power. What will change and what does it mean for the victims of car accidents? For years, the current Road Accident Fund (RAF) has been riddled with controversy - from lawyers like Bobroff taking much more than they are eligible to from the innocent victims of car accidents whose lives have been changed forever, to billions of rands of outstanding claims due to alleged mismanagement and incompetence at the organisation.
metadata.Further information: The proposed Bill for the Road Accident Benefit Scheme that will replace the RAF, will be signed into power at Parliament soon. It is an initiative from and will be implemented by the Department of Transport and the RAF is quick to defend that they are only following government's procedures and new initiative. The RAF is currently in a R144-billion deficit and has a backlog of 176-thousand outstanding cases. The new system will be managed by an Administrator and the backlog needs to be cleared, despite more cases that will be instituted due to the new Road Accident Benefit Scheme that also allow the person who was responsible for the accident to claim from the fund. This will ultimately increase the claim load and leave less money to be paid out to victims of car accidents who really need it to be cared for. The Road Accident Fund (RAF) was established in 1996 to protect the rights of innocent persons injured in accidents as a result of another’s negligent driving. The fund was designed to compensate victims for damages incurred, pain and suffering, medical expenses and loss of income, and also to protect those dependents who suffered loss of support due to a provider’s injury or death. The RAF is funded by fuel levies. For every rand paid for petrol, a percentage is set aside for the fund. The fund therefore should be well supported and maintained with continual growth as road use increases year by year. Those able to prove injuries and expenses incurred as a result of an accident that was not their fault, could apply and expect fair assessment and compensation for costs and/or loss of income to be paid out in a lump sum. The problems with RAF: However, over the years a number of problems developed with regard to the application process through the RAF. Chief of these included unacceptable delays in processing claims, often not at all unless the case was pursued by attorney. Delays of up to 55 months before a victim might receive compensation – and then only when professional assistance was sought by a claimant – were eroding the purpose and fairness of the ‘raison d’etre’ for the fund’s existence. Because of this incompetence, many claims would only be paid out if litigation was involved, resulting not only in extensive time delays but also unnecessary costs. This maladministration bled money from the fund, and compensation that should have been efficiently assessed and paid out in a reasonable time-span, was instead spent on time-consuming processes through the courts. So, undeniably, change was required. And this change has finally surfaced in the form of the Road Accident Benefit Scheme proposed to replace RAF. The draft RABS bill was published in May 2014. While seeking to institute a fairer spread of compensation to benefit the unemployed, or those earning below the Annual National Average Income (AANI), RABS brings with it a number of negative implications, such as: • All claims need to be submitted electronically in order to be considered. • The ‘No Fault’ system is supported – which means that the person who caused the accident will also be able to claim for injuries sustained. • If you don’t hear from RABS for 180 days after submitting your claim, your claim has been denied. • There is no lump sum payment – benefits are reduced to small monthly payments. • Loss of long-term ‘career path’ earnings are no longer considered – ie: loss of income (LOI) that would have been in your life had there been no accident, are not relevant. • LOI benefits will be based on only 75% of the claimant’s earnings prior to the accident. • Benefits are not inflation-linked nor guaranteed as benefits can be reviewed, revised or suspended at any time. • Claimants access to attorneys is limited, therefore the constitutional right to access the courts is denied. • The nature and extent of a victim’s medical treatment will be decided by the RABS Administrator. • There will be no general damage claims for pain and suffering. • There will be no financial assistance for any legal or administrative costs the victim may incur while trying process their claim. • Costs of obtaining medical and police reports will lie with the claimant – RABS will not refund these costs. • The claims of children, persons over 60 years of age, and persons earning over R220,000 pa, will be limited to emergency medical care only. • Funeral expenses will be limited to R10,000. • Benefits terminate on the death of the claimant, leaving any dependents without support. • Benefits terminate after 15 years or when the claimant reaches 60, whichever comes first. • Stringent rules will apply to qualify for long-term medical care – and will only be allowed from healthcare contractors specified by the RABS administration. •
